gist: The clean negative above survives a twelfth reading, but OpenClaw (read from source 2026-08-31) changes what it *means*. It is the first harness in this set that ships a general-purpose escaping wrapper — and still injects its context files raw.

item: Memory as a platform resource (read 2026-11-02)
gist: Added 2026-11-02 for the Keel memory proposal (`agent-design/keel/memory.md`). Everything above treats memory as a feature of one agent product.

item: Budget, and saying when it bit
gist: *Per-file cap: 32 KiB. Total cap: 64 KiB. Both are harness constants, not configuration. Codex's 32 KiB shared budget is the only budget in the field, and its failure mode is the one to avoid:

item: Escaping: nobody does it
gist: *Not one harness escapes, encodes, or sanitizes the body of a context file before splicing it into the prompt. A file containing `</INSTRUCTIONS>` closes Codex's envelope.

item: The memory-first systems (secondhand, not re-read this pass)
gist: These are memory products rather than agent harnesses. They are known from their papers and public docs; none was read from code for this document, and the claims below should be checked before being relied on.

item: Every field, and what it is for
gist: `sections[]`, not one blob — precedence (§1a), budgeting (§2), the run record (§10) and the write-protection set (§10a) all need per-unit granularity. A blob makes "which rule applied" unanswerable, which is the failure this whole document exists to avoid.

item: Three postures on authority
gist: The same class of file — a Markdown document any contributor can commit — is introduced to the model three incompatible ways: *Supreme. Claude Code: *"These instructions OVERRIDE any default behavior and you MUST follow them exactly as written."* *Subordinate on safety, superior on everything else.

item: Memory as an attack surface
gist: Consolidating a transcript means feeding attacker-influenceable text (tool output, fetched pages, third-party file contents) to a model that writes durable instructions read by every future session. Every source that built a background consolidator noticed:

item: Just-in-time loading for deeper files
gist: The harness already holds every repo section within the run's declared path scope — §1b's one call returns all of them, not just the root. So just-in-time loading is a reveal, not a read:

item: Skills: a catalog in the prompt, a body on demand
gist: Skills are the field's answer to "this instruction text is only relevant sometimes". The shape is the same in every implementation: a catalog of names and one-line descriptions is always in the prompt, and the body of `SKILL.md` enters context only when the model asks for it.

item: Retrieval: pasted in, pointed at, searched, or triggered
gist: Five retrieval modes, and most mature systems use two or three at once: Unconditionally injected into every prompt.

item: Inlining, and when not to
gist: `formats.md` §1's `<repo_context>` currently says: inline the root file "if one exists and is short enough to inline; otherwise its path only, and the model reads it itself". Made concrete: ≤ 32 KiB: inlined as a `<conventions>` block. > 32 KiB: the first 32 KiB inlined, truncation announced (§2).

item: Where it lands, and what that costs in cache
gist: Claude Code's is the one to read closely, because the two layers of framing contradict each other. The outer wrapper says: `<system-reminder>` As you answer the user's questions, you can use the following context: … IMPORTANT: this context may or may not be relevant to your tasks.

item: The channel that isn't memory: improvement requests
gist: There is a fourth thing an agent can do with something it learned, distinct from storing it, asking about it, or acting on it: hand it to a human who can fix the thing it is about.

item: Selection is the harness's job, and it is deterministic
gist: *Also not v1 — v1's harness appends what it receives. When selection arrives, this is where it belongs and what it must look like. The service returns everything that applies to `(repo, ref, team)`.

item: The review-tool loop: learning from humans instead of from yourself
gist: Review bots have the same problem in a different shape. They don't have a transcript worth mining — they have a stream of human reactions to their own output, which is a far cleaner training signal than an agent's self-assessment.

item: Who writes it: the working model, a background agent, or a human
gist: Three distinct authorship models, and the middle one is the newest and most interesting.
